title: Japanese Grammar — N5 complete, N4 core, production-first
goal: Grammar as pattern production, not rule recitation: every probe asks you to build or fix real sentences, blind-assessed. Follows the vault's Japanese method (Japanese/Resources.md): grammar refs are Yoku.bi / Morg systems; immersion is anime + jimaku subs; reading is the novel parser at GJ/Yotsuba level. Vocabulary deliberately lives in Anki (Kaishi 1.5k + mined words (no fixed frequency cutoff, per Resources.md)) — engram owns ONLY grammar patterns and their output; example words here are high-frequency vehicles, not vocab cards. Threshold arcs: particle role system, は/が, te-form hub, relative clauses.

jp-sentence-skeleton.claim: Japanese is SOV with particles doing the work English does with word order: the verb anchors the end, and は/が/を/に mark each noun's job. The sentence skeleton is [topic は] [context] [object を] [verb] — roles come from particles, not position.
jp-sentence-skeleton.probe: A friend who knows only English says 'you can't understand a Japanese sentence until you hear the last word.' Explain what's right about that intuition, what particles do instead of word order, and rearrange 私は本を読みます while keeping it grammatical — which parts can move and which cannot?
rubric: right intuition: the sentence-final verb is the anchor; everything before it sets up context
particles (は topic, が subject, を object, に target) assign roles, so pre-verb order is flexible for emphasis
本を can move before 私は or drop entirely; 読みます must stay last

viz.hint: Drag noun blocks around a sentence frame; watch role labels stick to the particles as blocks move.

jp-sentence-skeleton.transfer_probe: A log format tags every field with its role (ts=, user=, action=) instead of relying on column order, so shuffled columns still parse. What does that share with Japanese particles vs English word order — and which part of the log line plays the verb's anchoring role?

jp-copula.claim: だ/です is the 'is' of nouns and na-adjectives: だ plain, です polite, じゃない(です) negative, でした past. Register is a dial you choose per situation — plain form is what books, inner thoughts, and relative clauses use; です/ます is conversation with strangers.
jp-copula.probe: Produce four versions of 'It's a cat' — plain affirmative, polite affirmative, plain negative, polite past. Then answer: which form would you use inside a novel's narration, and why does the same choice matter for grammar (not just politeness)?
rubric: 猫だ / 猫です / 猫じゃない / 猫でした（or 猫じゃなかった）
narration uses plain form (だ) — it's the register of writing and thought
plain form is grammatically required inside clauses (relative clauses, before nouns) — です cannot attach there

jp-verb-groups.claim: Every verb sorts into one of three groups that decide ALL its conjugations: る-verbs (stem + る, stem ends in e/i row), う-verbs (dictionary form ends in u-row kana), and two irregulars (する, 来る). Misclassifying a verb corrupts every derived form — 食べる vs 飲む conjugate by different rules.
jp-verb-groups.probe: Sort these into groups and give each dictionary form's group-mate test: 食べる, 飲む, する, 見る, 読む, 来る, 帰る. Which one is the classic trap and why?
rubric: る-verbs: 食べる, 見る; う-verbs: 飲む, 読む, 帰る; irregulars: する, 来る
帰る is the trap: ends in -iru sound but is a う-verb (godan) — its forms follow 飲む's pattern, not 見る's
the reliable test: if the character BEFORE る is on the い/え row it's usually a る-verb, but exceptions like 帰る/走る must be memorized as words

jp-masu-polite.claim: The ます system is one uniform polite layer over any verb: ます present/future, ません negative, ました past, ませんでした past-negative. It never changes meaning — only register — and its regularity is why it's learned first while the plain forms underneath do the real grammatical heavy lifting.
jp-masu-polite.probe: Conjugate 食べる and 読む through all four ます forms. Then explain the paradox: why learn ます first if plain forms matter more?
rubric: 食べます／食べません／食べました／食べませんでした; 読みます／読みません／読みました／読みませんでした
same four endings attach to both verb groups unchanged — ます is fully regular
ます-first because it's safe everywhere socially and dead regular; but clauses (te-form, relatives, quoting) demand plain forms, so they're the real destination

practice.problem_frame: Conjugate any given verb through all four masu forms on demand.
practice.discriminates_from: Applying masu rules to irregulars wrongly (来ます, not 来るます).
practice.verify: Negative-past round trip: ませんでした reverts correctly to dictionary form.
error_bank: stem extraction errors on u-verbs
ました vs ませんでした mixing
irregular します/来ます mishandled

jp-particles-wa-ga.claim: は marks the TOPIC (what we're talking about — old information, contrastive scope), が marks the SUBJECT (new information, exhaustive answers to who/what, objects of existence/emotion). '私は犬が好き' uses both because 犬 is what 好き acts on within the topic 私. Choosing wrong doesn't break grammar — it breaks the information flow.
jp-particles-wa-ga.probe: Someone asks 誰が来た？ Answer correctly with が, then explain why answering with 田中さんは来ました sounds off. Then explain what 私は寿司が好きだ says about 寿司 vs 私, and give a context where 田中さんは来た WOULD be natural.
rubric: answer: 田中さんが来た — question-word subjects take が; は steals focus onto a topic nobody asked about
私は寿司が好きだ: 私 = topic/frame, 寿司 = the thing exhaustively liked (likes SUSHI, not other things)
田中さんは来た works when Tanaka is already the established topic ('As for Tanaka, he came') or as contrast (others didn't)

viz.hint: Two-stage spotlight: は lights the stage (topic), が spots the actor stepping on (new subject).

jp-particles-wa-ga.transfer_probe: Take three sentences from your immersion today that used が where you'd have guessed は (or vice versa), and reconstruct what information-status choice the speaker made.

jp-particle-o.claim: を marks the direct object — the thing the verb acts fully upon: パンを食べる. It also rides motion verbs of traversal (公園を散歩する — walking THROUGH the park) and departure (電車を降りる), where the noun is the path/route rather than a target.
jp-particle-o.probe: Explain the difference between 公園で散歩します and 公園を散歩します — both involve a park and walking, so what does each PARTICLE claim about the park? Give one more movement-verb + を example beyond the park (path crossed or departure point). Then produce 'I drink water every morning' in Japanese.
rubric: 公園を散歩する: the park is the route traversed (through-space); 公園で散歩する: the park is the venue where wandering happens
を with movement verbs = path/space crossed (道を歩く, 空を飛ぶ)
毎朝水を飲みます

jp-particles-ni-de.claim: に points at targets and fixed points: destination (学校に行く), time stamps (7時に起きる), location of existence (机の上に本がある), recipient (友達にあげる). で marks WHERE action happens and BY WHAT means: 図書館で勉強する, バスで行く, 日本語で書く. Existence takes に; activity takes で.
jp-particles-ni-de.probe: Fix the errors and justify each: (1) 東京で行きます (2) 7時で起きます (3) 机の上で本があります. Then translate: 'I study Japanese at the library with a dictionary.'
rubric: (1) 東京に行きます — destination takes に; (2) 7時に起きます — clock times take に; (3) 机の上に本があります — existence location takes に
rule of thumb: verb of being/targeted motion → に; verb of doing → で
図書館で日本語を勉強します、辞書を使って (or 辞書で acceptable at this level for 'by means of')

jp-particles-no-e.claim: の chains nouns left-to-right as modifiers: 私の本, 日本語の先生, 学校の近く — it's the universal 'of'/possessive/linker. へ/に mark direction of movement (日本へ行く), with へ emphasizing direction and に arrival/point.
jp-particles-no-e.probe: Unpack the noun chain 友達の母さんの車 into who owns what, then build 'my friend's older brother's bicycle' in Japanese. When would you pick へ over に for 'going to Osaka'?
rubric: friend's mother's car — each の attaches the left noun as modifier of the right one
友達のお兄ちゃんの自転車 (or 友達の兄の自転車)
大阪へ行く stresses toward-Osaka direction (e.g. stopping elsewhere possible); 大阪に行く treats Osaka as the arrival point — near-interchangeable in casual speech

jp-i-adjectives.claim: い-adjectives conjugate THEMSELVES like verbs: 高い → 高くない (neg), 高かった (past), 高くなかった (past-neg), 高くて (linking). The い IS the grammar — you never add です to make past tense (高かったです adds only politeness). Attributive position needs nothing: 高い山.
jp-i-adjectives.probe: Conjugate 忙しい into negative, past, past-negative, and te-linking forms. A friend writes 忙しいでした — diagnose the error precisely, then show how to make it polite correctly.
rubric: 忙しくない / 忙しかった / 忙しくなかった / 忙しくて
忙しいでした double-marks: い-adjectives carry their own tense; でした after い-stem is ungrammatical
polite past = 忙しかったです — politeness です stacks AFTER the adjective's own conjugation

practice.problem_frame: Conjugate any i-adjective into negative/past/past-neg/te-linking on demand.
practice.discriminates_from: Na-adjective patterns sneaking in (静かだった vs 高かった).
practice.verify: Check whether い is retained or dropped per form (なかった keeps the い of ない).
error_bank: 忙しいでした double-marking
dropping い before かった
いい→よかった irregular forgotten

jp-na-adjectives.claim: な-adjectives are nouns wearing an adjective costume: they take な when modifying a noun (静かな部屋) and behave exactly like nouns otherwise (静かだ, 静かじゃない, 静かでした). The な appears ONLY in attributive position — knowing where な shows up is the whole skill.
jp-na-adjectives.probe: A friend asks why 静かな部屋 is right but 静かだ部屋 and 静かなだ are wrong. Explain the two faces of na-adjectives, then conjugate 好き into negative and past politely.
rubric: before a noun: insert な (attributive); everywhere else: treat as noun with copula (静かだ/じゃない/でした)
静かだ部屋 wrongly stacks predicate form where attributive belongs; 静かなだ stacks な and だ in the same slot
好きじゃないです / 好きでした (past keeps noun behavior)

jp-questions.claim: Questions need no word-order change: add か to a statement (polite) or raise intonation (casual). Question words sit IN the sentence where the answer would go — 何を食べますか — and never take は; they take が as subjects. Each question word binds to its particle set (どこへ/どこで, 誰に, いつに✗).
jp-questions.probe: Turn 映画を見ます into yes/no questions in polite and casual style. Then ask 'what did you eat?', 'where did you buy it?', and 'with whom?' — watching which particles survive onto the question words.
rubric: 映画を見ますか / 映画を見る？
何を食べましたか；どこで買いましたか；誰と行きましたか
question words take が not は as subject (誰が来た), and いつ drops に (いつ行きます, not いつに行きます)

practice.problem_frame: Form yes/no and wh-questions from statements, attaching correct particles to question words.
practice.discriminates_from: English-style word-order inversion; は attached to question words.
practice.verify: Answer your own question and confirm the answer slot matches the question word's position.
error_bank: いつに over-marking
question word + は
casual intonation question written with stray か

jp-plain-past.claim: Plain past た is the backbone of real Japanese: 食べた/飲んだ/書いた/話した — built from the te-form (た = te with voicing). Plain forms are mandatory inside clauses, casual speech, and before nouns; the た/ない pair is the 'clause conjugation' everything else hangs from.
jp-plain-past.probe: Give plain past of 食べる, 飲む, 書く, する, 来る. Then explain why 昨日見た映画 is grammatical but 昨日見ました映画 is impossible — what job is 見た doing there?
rubric: 食べた / 飲んだ / 書いた / した / 来た（きた）
only PLAIN forms can modify nouns: 見た映画 = 'the movie I watched' — ました cannot attach inside a clause
た-form = te-form + tense voicing (飲んで→飲んだ); master te-form and past comes free

practice.problem_frame: Give plain past of any verb across all three groups on demand.
practice.verify: Ta-form equals te-form with final て→た / で→だ swap.
error_bank: 行った written as 行いた
irregular 来た/した missed
past-negative なかった forgotten

jp-plain-past.transfer_probe: Your diary entry and a police report describe the same day. Where do plain past forms live in each, and where are they mandatory (inside clauses, before nouns) regardless of how polite the surrounding text is?

jp-te-form.claim: Te-form is Japanese's universal clause connector — half of all grammar routes through it (progressive, requests, permission, linking, giving/receiving). Formation by group: る-verbs swap る→て (食べて); う-verbs split by final sound: う/つ/る→って, む/ぶ/ぬ→んで, く→いて (行く→行って special), ぐ→いで, す→して. Irregulars: して, 来て.
jp-te-form.probe: Give te-forms of: 食べる, 待つ, 飲む, 書く, 話す, 行く, 泳ぐ, する. Then state the one-sentence mnemonic for the う-verb sound map and name the famous exception.
rubric: 食べて / 待って / 飲んで / 書いて / 話して / 行って / 泳いで / して
map: う・つ・る→って; む・ぶ・ぬ→んで; く→いて; ぐ→いで; す→して
exception: 行く→行って (not 行いて) — pure memorization

viz.hint: Sort verbs by ending into five bins; each bin reveals its te-form transformation rule.

jp-te-form.transfer_probe: Pull five te-forms from your immersion reading this week, classify each against the sound map, and flag any your instinct got wrong before checking.

practice.problem_frame: Produce te-form of any verb; classify u-verbs by ending sound map.
practice.discriminates_from: Ru-verb shortcut applied to u-verbs (飲んで, never 飲みて).
practice.verify: Sound-map check: does the transformation match the final-kana bin?
error_bank: 行く→行いて
su-verbs getting んで
ru-verbs over-applying the sound map

jp-te-progressive.claim: ている fuses te-form + いる into two meanings the context picks: ongoing action (今食べている — eating now) and resultant state (結婚している — married, i.e. the ACT completed but STATE persists). With 〜ています it's the polite progressive; casual speech contracts to 〜てる.
jp-te-progressive.probe: Explain why 死んでいる does NOT mean 'is dying' but 'is dead'. Then produce: 'I am eating now' and 'I live in Tokyo' (state), casually and politely.
rubric: 死ぬ is instantaneous — once done, the RESULT persists: 死んでいる = in the state of having died = is dead
今食べています / 今食べてる；東京に住んでいます / 住んでる
durative verbs (住む, 持つ, 知る) default to resultant-state readings; action verbs (食べる, 走る) read as ongoing

jp-te-requests.claim: Requests and permission ride te-form: 〜てください (please do), 〜ないでください (please don't), 〜てもいいですか (may I?), 〜てはいけません (must not). The te-form hands the action over as a completed unit for the listener to react to — that's why ALL request grammar funnels through it.
jp-te-requests.probe: Ask permission to take a photo here, tell someone politely not to touch it, and forbid entry formally. Then explain what てもいい and てはいけ are each literally saying about the te-action.
rubric: 写真を撮ってもいいですか；触らないでください；入ってはいけません (or 入らないでください softer)
てもいい = even-if-you-do-(it's acceptable); てはいけ = if-you-do-(it's forbidden) — conditional logic under the politeness
negative requests flip to ない-form + で: ないでください

practice.problem_frame: Produce request/permission/prohibition forms from plain actions on demand.
practice.discriminates_from: Register slips between てはいけない and ちゃいけない; ないで vs なくて.
practice.verify: Flip request to prohibition and confirm morphology flips te ↔ nai-de correctly.
error_bank: 触ってはいください nonsense blend
over-complete answers to てもいいですか
negative request built with なくてで

jp-te-linking.claim: Te-form chains clauses like commas with logic: sequential action (朝起きて、コーヒーを飲んで、出かけた), cause (雨が降って、試合は中止になった), and manner (走って来た — came running). The connector is logically vague — sequence OR cause OR means — and context decides, which is also its danger.
jp-te-linking.probe: Translate 'I got up at seven, ate breakfast, and went to school' using te-chains. Then explain the ambiguity risk in 彼に電話して、謝った — what two readings exist and how would you force the causal one?
rubric: 七時に起きて、朝ご飯を食べて、学校に行きました
電話して、謝った reads as sequence (called THEN apologized) or cause (apologized BECAUSE called) — te doesn't say which
force causality with から/ので: 電話したから、謝った — explicit connectives override te's vagueness

practice.problem_frame: Chain three-plus clauses into one sentence with te-forms, controlling sequence vs cause reading.
practice.discriminates_from: Using te where explicit cause (から/ので) is required.
practice.verify: Read aloud: temporal order survives the chaining; final clause carries proper predicate tense.
error_bank: te-chaining non-sequential events confusingly
sentence ending in bare te-form
tense inconsistency across the chain

jp-existence-aru-iru.claim: Existence splits by animacy: いる for things that move themselves (people, animals), ある for everything else (objects, events, abstracts). Pattern: [location に] [thing が] ある/いる — note が, not は, marks the existing thing. 部屋に猫がいる / 問題がある.
jp-existence-aru-iru.probe: Translate: 'There's a cat on the desk' and 'There's a problem with my computer.' Why does 猫がいます take が while earlier you learned topics take は? What does 机の上に猫はいません imply instead?
rubric: 机の上に猫がいます；コンピューターに問題があります
existence presents NEW information — new subjects take が; は would topicalize the cat as known context
机の上に猫はいません implies contrast: no CAT there (but maybe something else) — は adds its contrastive flavor even in negatives

jp-counters.claim: Japanese counts nouns through counters matched to shape/category: 枚 flat (paper, plates), 本 long/cylindrical (pens, bottles), 匹 small animals, 人 people (with irregulars 一人/二人), 台 machines, 冊 bound books. The generic つ series (一つ、二つ…) handles unknown shapes — and counting people/round-objects has irregular readings you just memorize.
jp-counters.probe: Count in Japanese: 3 sheets of paper, 2 pens, 4 dogs, 1 person, 5 books. Which counter saves you when you don't know an object's category, and what are the irregular readings in the people series?
rubric: 紙三枚 / ペン二本 / 犬四匹 / 一人 / 本五冊
つ-series (一つ、二つ、三つ…) is the shape-agnostic fallback
people: 一人（ひとり）、二人（ふたり）、then 三人… — first two readings are irregular

jp-time-expressions.claim: Time splits into point vs duration: absolute points take に (7時に, 月曜日に) but relative words (今日, 明日, 最近) drop it; duration takes 間 (二時間) and frequency uses 回 (週三回). まで/から extend to time naturally: 9時から5時まで働く.
jp-time-expressions.probe: Fix where needed: (1) 今日に学校に行きます (2) 三時間勉強しました (3) 週に三回ジムに行きます. Then say 'I work from 9 to 5' and explain why 今日 rejects に.
rubric: (1) 今日、学校に行きます — relative time words take no に; (2)(3) correct as-is
9時から5時まで働きます
に marks a POINT on a shared calendar/clock; 今日/明日/去年 are defined relative to speech moment, not a clock point

jp-adverbs-degree.claim: Degree adverbs pair with polarity: とても/かなり scale UP positives, while あまり and ぜんぜん grammatically REQUIRE negatives (あまり美味しくない — not very tasty; ぜんぜん分からない — don't understand at all). Adverbs sit flexibly before the element they scale, and ちょっと softens refusals more than it measures quantity.
jp-adverbs-degree.probe: Translate with correct polarity: 'This movie is very interesting', 'It's not very interesting', 'I don't understand at all'. Then explain why あまり美味しい is broken and what social work ちょっと does in ちょっと…
rubric: この映画はとても面白い / あまり面白くない / ぜんぜん分かりません
あまり/ぜんぜん are negative-polarity items — they license and demand the ない
ちょっと trailing off = soft refusal ('it's a bit… difficult') — pragmatic softener beyond literal quantity

jp-kara-made.claim: から/made bracket ranges in space AND time AND abstract provenance: 9時から5時まで, 東京から大阪まで, 彼から聞いた (heard FROM him). から doubles as 'because' joining clauses (高いから、買いません), making it one of the highest-frequency connectors in the language.
jp-kara-made.probe: Say: 'The station is from here to the university' (range), 'I bought it because it was cheap'. Then explain the difference between 高いから、買いません and 高いので、買いません at the nuance level.
rubric: 駅はここから大学までです；安かったから、買いました
から = subjective/direct reason (blunt, personal judgment); ので = softer, objective-seeming — politeness strategy in explanations/refusals
both join full clauses; から can also end a sentence alone as justification

jp-kedo-ga.claim: Contrast joins via が/けど/けれど: Aが、B (but), 〜のに (although — with frustration/friction nuance), 〜ても (even if). Casual speech loves sentence-final けど as a softener ('…, though'). The connector choice encodes attitude: が neutral, のに personal grievance, ても concessive-conditional.
jp-kedo-ga.probe: Join with the RIGHT contrastive and justify: 'I studied, but I couldn't answer' (neutral) vs 'I studied so much, and yet I couldn't answer' (frustrated). Then soften a refusal with sentence-final けど.
rubric: 勉強しましたが、答えられませんでした (neutral が)
たくさん勉強したのに、答えられませんでした (のに carries the let-down/frustration)
行きたいんですけど、ちょっと… — trailing けど leaves the refusal unsaid but understood

jp-relative-clauses.claim: Relative clauses precede the noun and use PLAIN forms, keeping their particles intact: 昨日買った本 (the book I bought yesterday), 母が作った料理 (dish that mom made). The clause is a modifier machine — the modified noun fills whichever role the clause leaves open, and subject-inside-clause switches to が.
jp-relative-clauses.probe: Build: 'the person who came yesterday', 'the movie I watched with a friend', 'the book I borrowed FROM the library'. In the last one, where did 図書館's particle go and why is 図書館を借りた本 wrong?
rubric: 昨日来た人；友達と見た映画；図書館で借りた本
borrowing happens AT the library (venue → で survives inside the clause); を belongs to 本 which has moved outside as head noun
whole-clause-before-noun order is rigid; inside, the clause keeps normal SOV with particles

viz.hint: Slot-machine: assemble clause pieces left of a noun block; watch the gap-filler highlight which particle stayed home.

jp-relative-clauses.transfer_probe: Find one relative clause in your novel reading, mark where the head noun's original particle went, and rebuild the sentence as two separate sentences.

jp-nominalizer-no-koto.claim: の and こと turn clauses into nouns so they can be discussed: 料理を作るのが好き (I like cooking-it), 日本語を習うことは難しい. の is concrete/perceptual and the only choice after 好き/嫌い/見える; こと is abstract/factual and required after 言う/思う/できる-style predicates. The explanation pattern のだ/んです rides on this nominalization.
jp-nominalizer-no-koto.probe: Choose の or こと and justify: (1) 泳ぐ＿が好きです (2) 毎日運動する＿は大切です (3) 遅れた＿は電車が止まったからです (explanation). What does んです add to 遅れたんです vs plain 遅れました？
rubric: (1) の — perception/affect predicates take の; (2) こと — abstract proposition as topic; (3) の — explanatory のだ pattern
rule of thumb: perceived/concrete → の; stated/abstract fact → こと; some predicates accept either with nuance shift
state what んです adds to 遅れたんです versus plain 遅れました: it frames the statement as explanation/context-sharing

jp-potential.claim: Potential forms express CAN/ability: る-verbs → −られる (食べられる), う-verbs → e-row + る (飲む→飲める), する→できる, 来る→こられる. The object may flip を→が (日本語が話せる) because potential is intransitive-ish — the ability arises in you. All potential verbs conjugate as る-verbs thereafter.
jp-potential.probe: Make potential forms of 話す, 食べる, 泳ぐ, する. Then explain the を→が shift in 日本語を話します vs 日本語が話せます, and why 無理 — not できない — often sounds more natural for 'I can't (manage it)'.
rubric: 話せる / 食べられる / 泳げる / できる
potential re-frames the event as capacity arising in the subject, so the object takes が (subject-of-emotion/existence pattern)
できない states logical impossibility; 無理 conveys practical/beyond-my-capacity — everyday speech prefers it for tasks

practice.problem_frame: Convert any verb to potential form and build an ability sentence with ga-marked object.
practice.discriminates_from: Passive られる vs potential られる for ru-verbs (context disambiguates).
practice.verify: Potential forms conjugate as ru-verbs thereafter — test a negative: 食べられない.
error_bank: keeping を rigidly where が is natural
泳げる misformed from 泳ぐ
できる mishandled in compound-noun ability statements

jp-volitional-let.claim: Volitional marks intent and invitation: う-verbs → おう-row (飲もう), る-verbs → よう (食べよう), しましょう polite 'let's'. Alone it's casual 'let's/I think I'll'; と思っています after volitional = sustained intention (行こうと思っている — I'm planning to go).
jp-volitional-let.probe: Say casually: 'let's eat!', 'I'll buy it (decided just now)'. Then express a PLAN you've been holding: 'I'm thinking of going to Japan next year' — which construction carries the sustained intention, and how does it differ from a spur-of-the-moment 行こう？
rubric: 食べよう！；これ、買おう
来年日本に行こうと思っています — volitional+と思う+ている = deliberated, held intention
bare 行こう = spontaneous invitation/decision in the moment; と思っている version reports a standing plan

practice.problem_frame: Produce volitional forms for spontaneous decisions and sustained intentions (volitional + と思っている).
practice.discriminates_from: ましょう politeness level vs casual おう/よう.
practice.verify: U-verb volitional lands on the ou-row: test 飲む→飲もう.
error_bank: 食べろう (wrong; must be 食べよう)
volitional+と思う conflated with たい-desire
する→しよう missed

jp-passive.claim: Passive −れる/−られる shifts focus to the receiver: 犬に噛まれた (I was bitten BY a dog — agent takes に). Japanese passives shine in the ADVERSITY use: 先生に来られて困った (the teacher came and I was put out) — an event happened TO you without direct action on you, expressing suffered inconvenience English can't.
jp-passive.probe: Convert to passive: 誰かが私のかばんを盗んだ. Then explain what happens literally in 先生に宿題を忘れられた, what it expresses emotionally, and why English has no clean equivalent.
rubric: かばんは（誰かに）盗まれた — agent optional, marked by に
the teacher's coming happened independently, and I suffered its consequences — adversity passive packages 'inconvenienced by someone else's act'
English requires awkward padding ('had my homework forgotten by...' fails); Japanese grammaticalizes the victim perspective

jp-causative.claim: Causative −させる/−せる makes someone DO something (母に野菜を食べさせた — made him eat vegetables; forced → に, permitted/let → を on the object). Stack it with passive for させられる (be MADE to do — the drudgery form): 残業させられた (was made to work overtime).
jp-causative.probe: Distinguish forced vs allowed in causative marking: 息子に野菜を食べさせた vs 息子にゲームをさせてやった — what changed grammatically? Then complain in Japanese: 'I was made to work Saturday.'
rubric: causee takes に; when the verb already has a を-object, keep causee に and object を (母は息子に野菜を食べさせた); permission vs coercion is signaled by benefactive helpers (させてやる/てあげる = let, plain させた = made)
土曜日に働かせられた / 働かされた — causative-passive = compelled against will
させられる is THE complaint form: suffering + compulsion in one morphology

jp-give-receive.claim: Benefactives encode WHO benefits from whose perspective: あげる (I/we give outward), くれる (someone gives TO me/my side — gratitude built in), もらう (I receive/have someone do). Te-form versions package favors: 書いてくれる (they kindly wrote it for me), 書いてもらった (I had them write it). Choosing the wrong verb misassigns the favor's direction — a real social error.
jp-give-receive.probe: Your friend taught you Japanese. Say it two ways — them-as-giver (gratitude-flavored) and you-as-receiver. Then explain why 友達が教えてくれてありがとう is natural but 友達が教えてあげてありがとう is a social bug.
rubric: 友達が（私に）教えてくれた / 友達に教えてもらった
くれる views flow INTO my side and carries built-in gratitude; あげる views flow OUTWARD from my side — thanking someone for giving outward is backwards
もらう frames me as beneficiary-controller ('I had/got them to teach me')

jp-transitive-intransitive.claim: Japanese pairs verbs across transitivity with recurring sound patterns (開ける/開く, 出す/出る, 落とす/落ちる): the transitive takes を (ドアを開ける — I open it), the intransitive takes が (ドアが開いた — it opened). Picking the wrong half misattributes agency — 開けた claims YOU did it; 開いた reports it happened.
jp-transitive-intransitive.probe: Pick the right verb + particle: 'I opened the window' vs 'the window opened (by itself)'. Give the partner of 落ちる and of 壊れる, then explain why ドアを開いた is doubly wrong.
rubric: 窓を開けました / 窓が開きました
落とす (drop something) partners 落ちる; 壊す partners 壊れる
ドアを開いた mixes transitive particle with intransitive verb — agency claim (を) plus no-agent verb (開いた) contradict

jp-conditionals-tara-ba.claim: Four conditionals, four flavors: たら (default/general 'when/if' — most common), ば (logical/statement-of-condition), と (automatic consequence — whenever X, Y invariably), なら (topic-limiting 'if it's the case that'). と states machine-like inevitability; なら responds to known context; たら covers narrative future/when.
jp-conditionals-tara-ba.probe: Pick the conditional and defend: (1) 'Press this button and (always) the light turns on' (2) 'If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home' (3) 'If you're going to Osaka, the Shinkansen is fastest' (4) 'If you mix those chemicals, they WILL explode.' Map each to と/たら/なら/ば and justify your mapping.
rubric: (1) と — automatic invariant results; (2) たら — hypothetical/narrative future; (3) なら — builds on the hearer’s stated plan; (4) と/ば — lawlike result
たら is the safe default; と refuses volitional/willful main clauses (×雨が降ると、家にいます)
なら licenses advice/recommendations keyed to the mentioned topic

jp-appearance-sou-you.claim: Two そう with different sources: stem+そう = appearance from direct observation (美味しそう — looks tasty; drop the final い), plain-form+そう = hearsay/report (美味しいそうだ — I hear it's tasty). ようだ/みたい expresses inference from evidence; らしい reputation/hearsay-at-one-remove. Choosing the wrong evidential misreports HOW you know — Japanese grammar makes epistemology obligatory.
jp-appearance-sou-you.probe: Your friend says the ramen shop is good. Report it three ways: (a) you heard it from them, (b) you walked past and smelled it, (c) you tried it and conclude it's probably good. Which evidential fits each, and why is 美味しいそう (appearance-form) impossible for (a)?
rubric: (a) 美味しいそうだ/らしい — hearsay そう attaches to plain form; (b) 美味しそう — appearance そう attaches to adjective STEM (い dropped); (c) 美味しいようだ/みたい — inference from experience
appearance-そう requires firsthand perceptual grounds; using it for hearsay misreports your evidence source
evidentials are grammatical obligations in Japanese — every reported claim encodes its channel

capstone.claim: You can USE Japanese Grammar — N5 complete, N4 core, production-first in your own work, not just explain it.
capstone.probe: Build the thing. In your real repo, your real notes, your real argument — produce something that only works if you actually understand Japanese Grammar — N5 complete, N4 core, production-first. Your stated goal: Grammar as pattern production, not rule recitation: every probe asks you to build or fix real sentences, blind-assessed. Follows the vault's Japanese method (Japanese/Resources.md): grammar refs are Yoku.bi / Morg systems; immersion is anime + jimaku subs; reading is the novel parser at GJ/Yotsuba level. Vocabulary deliberately lives in Anki (Kaishi 1.5k + mined words (no fixed frequency cutoff, per Resources.md)) — engram owns ONLY grammar patterns and their output; example words here are high-frequency vehicles, not vocab cards. Threshold arcs: particle role system, は/が, te-form hub, relative clauses.. Ship it, then explain which concept made which decision.
rubric: the artifact exists and works (or the argument stands on its own)
names at least two concepts from this topic that DECIDED something in it
identifies where the model broke down or needed more than the topic gave

jp-keigo-system.claim: Keigo is architecture, not decoration: three registers (sonkeigo raises the other, kenjougo lowers the self, teineigo polishes the sentence), the core irregular pairs (suru/nasaru/itasu, iku/irassharu/mairu, taberu/meshiagaru/itadaku, miru/goran-ni-naru/haiken-suru), and the decision rule — who acts, who benefits, what the relationship demands — applied before any verb is chosen.
jp-keigo-system.probe: First state the three-register architecture (sonkeigo raises the other, kenjougo lowers the self, teineigo polishes the sentence). Then: your teacher hands you a book. Say it three ways (receiving as equal, receiving from a superior with humility, describing the teacher giving to someone else) using the correct irregular pairs - and for each utterance, state the rule before choosing the verb by justifying it with who-acts plus who-benefits plus relationship.
rubric: three registers named with the raise-other/lower-self/polish-sentence architecture
scenario verbs handled with the correct pairs inside the utterances (morau->itadaku, kureru->kudasaru, plus one sonkeigo/kenjougo demonstration) - no credit for context-free recital
each utterance justified by who-acts plus who-benefits plus relationship - rule before verb

viz.hint: Actor-to-beneficiary arrow diagram; slider morphs one sentence across plain, teineigo, sonkeigo, kenjougo.
